messages.subject: mixed effects models & Unmarked
messages.body_plain:
Unmarked Group,

I want to study bird population trends through time, but am working with an unbalanced design where sites vary among years.  From the literature it appears this analysis is do-able using mixed effect models where the year effect can be estimated while controlling for the site effect.  My understanding is that this sort of model cannot be implemented in Unmarked.  I thought I could try to combine n-mixture modeling in Unmarked and mixed effect modeling as follows:

1. Run n-mixture models in Unmarked using pcount
2. Use the best model to estimate densities using ranef()
3. Use parametric bootstrapping to create a dataset of 200 simulated density estimates
4. Run linear mixed effects models using the estimated densities as the response, determining the effect of year (fixed effect) while accounting for the effects of sites (random effect)
5. Repeat mixed effect models for each of the 200 simulated densities, calculating a 95% confidence interval for the year coefficient.

Does anyone have thoughts on this approach?  Its legitimacy or alternatives?

Mike Worland

messages.subject_clean: Estimating site-specific population sizes along an altitudinal gradient
messages.body_plain:
I must start off by congratulating the creators of "unmarked". It has proven indispensable to most of my analysis.
I should also congratulate everyone present on this group, the vast reservoir of discussions has helped the likes of me a lot to get started.

For my PhD, the ultimate aim is a comparative analysis of diversity profiles of birds and hawkmoths (Lepidoptera:Sphingidae) along an elevational gradient spanning 3000m.

The bird data consists of replicated transect counts (12 replicates) at 13 elevations. I am thinking of using the N-mix model to estimate site specific population sizes for each species, and using these estimates for subsequent beta-diversity analysis (nestedness,turnover,relative abundance patterns etc)

I have come across studies where-in these models were just used to reflect on the relationship between detection probability and/or abundance with different covariates and comment on the explanatory power of one co-variate over another by model selection.

I have yet to come across a study which uses the N-mix model to estimate site-specific population sizes and use these over observed abundances for answering higher level questions of community assembly. If anyone could share with me any reference I would be eternally grateful.

What I have managed to do thus far is generate Nmix results for each individual species' data (looping over a list object) using elevation as the site level covariate :
           > Nmix_results[[i]] <- pcount(~1~Elevation,data=List_Element[[i]])

Quite predictably, I ran into our old friend Mr. Hessian. I scaled the siteCovs (as per a suggestion in a previous post) and the issue was resolved.

I then extracted site-specific abundance estimates (again thanks to a previous suggestion on this group) as follows:
              > Abund_Estimates[[i]] <- ranef(Nmix_results[[i]])

I am weary on the use of "Ranef" here, mostly because I am not quite confident of what it does. Could someone suggest an alternative, or justify my use?
My thesis advisor is not very well versed with these models (neither am I) and I would be eternally grateful if someone can give me a thumbs-up regarding whether I am headed in the right direction here.

Also, the data on hawkmoths consists of repeated sampling at 13 elevations (at least 5 instances at each elevation). The moths were not collected during the process, only photographed. Associated covariates can be date/lunar stage for obsCovs and elevation for sitesCovs.
Again, am I right here in using N-mix model for moth data? They have much shorter life spans, but the entire study was well within the shortest possible life span.

So, to summarize, I have 3 questions :
1. Comparing observed relative abundance patterns with estimated relative abundance patterns : does it make any sense?
2. Is "ranef" the function that can help me extract estimated population sizes from pcount results?
3. Can pcount be used for a light-trapping study where moths were not collected/trapped, only photographed and released?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

>
> I have yet to come across a study which uses the N-mix model to estimate site-specific population sizes and use these over observed abundances for answering higher level questions of community assembly. If anyone could share with me any reference I would be eternally grateful.

I feel as though I've seen community-level Nmix models used in community settings (calculating Hill #'s, etc.), but I can't seem to find anything immediately--the closest thing that immediately pops up is: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12296/abstract.  Others may have alternative ideas?

>
> I am weary on the use of "Ranef" here, mostly because I am not quite confident of what it does. Could someone suggest an alternative, or justify my use?
> My thesis advisor is not very well versed with these models (neither am I) and I would be eternally grateful if someone can give me a thumbs-up regarding whether I am headed in the right direction here.

If lambda represents the expected abundance at a site, the values associated with ranef are the empirical Bayes estimates of the latent variables/site-specific abundances...kind of the best guess for actual abundance at sites given the parameter estimates. To me, makes way more sense to use these values than expected values.

>
> 1. Comparing observed relative abundance patterns with estimated relative abundance patterns : does it make any sense?

 I don't quite know what this means.  Plugging the finite-sample abundance estimates into some subsequent analysis makes more sense than plugging expected abundance into a higher level analysis.In an ideal world, one might formulate a model in which variance in richness/turnover would be explicitly modeled (something kind of sensu the recent paper by Simone Tenan et al.: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/2041-210X.12719/abstract). If the idea is to try to look at residual differences between estimates of expected or realized abundance to say something about species associations, maybe something a joint species model would be useful (e.g., http://www.cell.com/trends/ecology-evolution/abstract/S0169-5347(15)00240-2).

>

>
> 3. Can pcount be used for a light-trapping study where moths were not collected/trapped, only photographed and released?

Pcount (N-mixture model) does not require that organisms are collected/trapped, only that observation is a binomial process (y is expected to be N*p). If your approach actually uses photography to identify individuals, multinomial observation models provide a little more flexibility for considering individual level variability in detection. If individual moths are double-counted within a sample, then the binomial process is not appropriate (y can be greater than N).

Cheers,

John

Hi Pat,

If you add -1 to each component of the formula you'll remove the intercepts and obtain a "means" instead of an "effects" parameterization. Right now your level 1 of each factor is represented by the intercept, and the other coefficients represent the estimated differences between those levels and the intercept. Removing the intercept gives you the mean estimates for each factor level.

Dear Sofia,

There are a few points of views on the issue when you don't have a global model (also check other posts on the list). To check model fit, you could use 1) the most parsimonious model, 2) the entire set of models, 3) a group of models with the majority of the Akaike weight, or 4) check the fit for each subglobal model as in Burnham and Anderson (2002, section 6.5.1).

The first option is the quickest, although model ranking can change when modifying c-hat and you can end up with a model different than the one you used to assess fit. The second systematic approach takes longer, but could be done in parallel on different cores. The third approach is somewhere in between, but I've never seen it implemented. I'd recommend the fourth approach, if possible.

Sofia, once you settle on a c-hat value, you can just feed it into most functions in the AICcmodavg package with the c.hat argument to do model selection or multimodel inference.

Hope it helps,

Marc

Hi Eunbi,

Log(gamma) here = B0+B1*area2+B2*dates+B3*dates^2....thus, gamma = exp(B0+B1*area2+B2*dates+B3*dates^2). It is the linear combination (see linearComb) that must be backtransformed in order to express gamma in real units, but the directional effect is best interpreted on the link (log) scale. Eg (ignoring date), with area2=0, gamma = exo(0.916) = ~2.5; with area2=1, gamma=exp(0.916 - 4.858)= ~0.025. In both cases, gamma is positive (which it has to be given the link), but area2 has a negative effect on the parameter.

Cheers,

John

Not that there's some secret knowledge out there that can't be publicly disclosed (or maybe there is, but I don't know about it), but the philosophy of scientific inquiry is a pretty broad topic.

Hi Shaun. I agree w John, regarding "camera" as a covariate on lambda: if it doesn't make sense as a biological hypothesis representing reality on the ground, then it shouldn't be a competing model, and likewise for any covariates. I'm not aware of any rule or justification always necessitating a fully "nested" model set containing all possible combinations of covariates. In my opinion, model sets should represent competing hypotheses developed to answer specific questions and be given thorough consideration before any models are fit (ie, "a priori" models). Regarding interactions, I'm under the impression that they are sometimes or often avoided because some find them more difficult to program and interpret, but I often find them to be the most informative components of a model. I'd wager a bet that interactions are present far more often than not in biological systems and data.

I found David Anderson's Model-based Inferences in the Life Sciences really useful as a grad student, as far as understanding both the quantitative and conceptual basis for building sets of competing models that most effectively answer the questions posed. It's a bit less technical than Burnham and Anderson's Model Selection and Multimodel Inference. Like John said, the wealth of literature on model inference is extensive. Happy hunting.

Matt

messages.body_plain:
Hello unmarked friends,

Question about violations of the assumptions of the dynamic occupancy model

Goal of my study: estimate temporal effects and survey length effects on the detection probability of occupied nests of Chimney Swift. We want to know this to inform protocols to effectively detect occupied chimneys...

Methods: We recorded the presence (1)/absence (0) of Chimney Swifts entering or exiting nest sites every 10 min within a 60 survey. So encounter histories look like ... 001011 for example. We repeated this survey at 47 nests 3 to four times over the nesting season. So this is a dynamic occupancy design but with only one year.

I have gone ahead with a colext model, but became concerned that the sampling occasions are NOT independent, which would be a violation of an assumption for dynamic occupancy models (Kéry 2012 colext vignette; pg. 3). So the real question is “are the 10-min intervals within a 60-min survey independent?” Within a survey, the encounter histories average 1.3 detections. This is due to the relatively long foraging bouts between nest visits, but mean detections across all intervals are constant (~0.3)... so... are the 10-min intervals independent? If not, would a better route be to conform my data to fit a removal occupancy model (i.e., NAs after the first detection)?

Many thanks to this wonderful group!

Myles

messages.subject: Re: AICc vs. likelihood ratio
messages.body_plain:
I recommend the sidebars in the gentle intro to MARK (ch. 4) as a quick read about IC and LRT: AIC will select the same models as the LRT at a very specific alpha (greater than 0.05 when few parameters are in a model, but declines in a decelerating fashion as K increases).  AICc induces a stronger penalty on model complexity than AIC because the cost of an additional parameter increases with small sample size. Defining n is not always straight-forward for many models, or n may differ for different parameters (the MacKenzie et al. 2006 book talks about this). The choice of some IC or regularization technique for choosing a model or ranking models is the practitioner's decision (you might prefer LASSO, BIC, etc.).  A broader question is whether you are fine with using the most supported model or have some desire to account for uncertainty in the selection of the most supported model and model average (appropriately! see Cade 2015): AIC(c) allows this; the LRT does not.

All results presented suggest m4 is the 'best' or 'most supported' model out of the ones presented. Your certainty in m4 as the best is a subjective decision that is similar to choosing alpha = 0.10, or 0.05, or 0.00001, or other value.  You have to decide to accept some risk that you are wrong in one way vs. another.

messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] What is K in pcount?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Adrian,

K is not a model parameter and not anything of biological importance either. You can think of it as simply a tuning "parameter" of the likelihood maximisation, nothing more. Technically, it is the upper bound of the summation over the possible values of N in the integrated likelihood that is maximised to obtain the MLEs.

But K has to be made big enough that the results (i.e., the estimates) won't be affected by your choice (i.e., won't change appreciably for instance when you make K even bigger). When your estimates keep changing when you make K bigger, then this indicates that the parameters are not estimable for your data set. We don't usually find this problem with the Poisson or the ZIP mixtures, BUT IT IS FREQUENTLY A PROBLEM WITH THE NEGBIN MIXTURE. When fitting Nmix models (using gmultimix() and especially with pcount()) we should always make a couple of tests of whether our parameters are identifiable by refitting the model with a bigger value of K.

Attached is what Royle, in his Biometrics paper in 2004, says on this this (on page 110, top left, of the paper).

Best wishes  --  Marc

messages.subject: Binary Indicator for Competition Covariate
messages.body_plain:
To my fellow occupancy analysts,

I'm trying to aproximate the co-occurrence of two species using MacKenzie's 2-species model, and am interested in assessing to what extent (if any) the species are in competition with one another. A simple solution to this, I would assume, would be to include a binary covariate indicating sites where both species were present and then assessing whether or not the model containing this covariate is the best model. My concern, is that there is a limited number (roughly 20%) of sites where the species do co-occur. Therefore, my expectation is that this covariate will falsely describe much more of the variance than it normally would assuming there were more sites where the species co-occurred. Any helpful suggestions on how I might get around this problem?

Thanks,

Josh

Dear Josh,
It is my understanding that the 2-species models of MacKenzie (2004), Richmond (2010), and others are not yet implemented in 'unmarked', but I am sure someone will correct me if I'm wrong or if that is in the works.

If both species are detected imperfectly, it will be difficult to create a covariate that *perfectly* measures co-occurrence. However, building encounter histories for each species and modeling detection explicitly may offer some alternatives. See a useful discussion here  <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/richmond$202010%7Csort:relevance/unmarked/SsCntWZjuGI/y24CNui5BgAJ>for more thoughts.

I've used the Richmond parameterization (which is more stable for use with covariates) in MARK (it's also available in PRESENCE), and you can derive a species interaction factor (SIF; described in Richmond 2010) that may provide the inference you're interested in.

Best,
Brittany
